name: Spice.ai OSS
summary: A single-binary SQL engine in Rust, built on DataFusion and Arrow, that federates queries across databases, warehouses and lakes, keeps hot datasets in a local accelerated copy, and adds search and LLM APIs on top.
intro: Spice runs as one Rust binary (`spiced`) next to an application, as a sidecar, a standalone service or a cluster. You list datasets in a YAML file, `spicepod.yaml`: a PostgreSQL table, Parquet files in S3, an Iceberg catalog, a Databricks or Snowflake table, and so on from about 30 connectors. Applications then query them all with SQL over HTTP, Arrow Flight SQL, JDBC, ODBC or ADBC. Apache DataFusion, which works on Apache Arrow’s in-memory columnar format, plans and runs the queries. For a dataset left in place, Spice pushes as much of the query as it can down to the source. That keeps the data where it is, but the slowest source sets the latency of a join.

The main idea is acceleration. For any dataset you can turn on a local copy, held in memory as Arrow, in an embedded DuckDB or SQLite file, or in Spice Cayenne, its own engine built on the Vortex columnar format. Spice keeps that copy fresh by reloading it on a schedule (`full`), appending new rows (`append`) or applying change data capture (`changes`). It reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, the MySQL binlog, MongoDB change streams or DynamoDB Streams directly, with no Kafka or Debezium in between. Queries then hit the local copy instead of the source, and a results cache answers repeated queries from memory. The project describes this as an active cache, or a CDN for databases.

On top of the data it adds AI features: an OpenAI-compatible API in front of hosted or local models, embeddings, vector, full-text and hybrid search as SQL table functions, text-to-SQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Version 1.0 was declared stable in January 2025 and 2.0 in June 2026, which made distributed queries on Apache Ballista and the Cayenne accelerator generally available; v2.3.2 came out in September 2026. The runtime is Apache 2.0. Spice AI, Inc. builds it and sells Spice Cloud, a managed service, and Spice.ai Enterprise, and a few connectors (ODBC, ScyllaDB, NFS, Elasticsearch) ship only in Enterprise builds unless you compile them in yourself.
strengths: One SQL endpoint over many sources, with query push-down, so an application doesn’t need a driver and a pipeline per database
Hot data served from a local copy next to the app, in memory or on disk, kept fresh by refreshes or direct CDC from PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB or DynamoDB
Small enough to run one instance per application or tenant: a single binary of about 140 MB, configured in one YAML file
Retrieval, search and LLM calls in the same engine as the data, through OpenAI-compatible and MCP interfaces
limits: Uneven maturity: core connectors are stable, but Kafka, Spark and SQL Server are beta, GCS and ClickHouse alpha, the SQLite accelerator a release candidate, and the vector engines alpha

Accelerated copies need memory or disk (the docs suggest at least 1.5 times the dataset size), and if a source’s schema changes while Spice is running, refreshes fail until it restarts or schema detection is turned on
Federated joins across many sources slow down, since the slowest source bounds the query; the docs recommend accelerating such joins instead
A young, single-vendor project whose headline benchmarks (for example against DuckDB and Spark) are the company’s own

story: Luke Kim and Phillip LeBlanc, who had built developer tools at Microsoft and GitHub, founded Spice AI in 2021. Kim said that while at Microsoft he had become convinced decision-making AI would matter to many applications, yet developers had no platform for it. The first Spice.ai, released as an alpha in August 2021, was an “open source runtime and distribution system for time series AI”: a runtime written in Go and Python that learned from streams of time-series data and served recommendations to apps over HTTP.

In February 2024, with version 0.7, the company replaced it with an all-new implementation in Rust. The new runtime dropped the built-in AI training engine and dashboard, which moved to the hosted Spice.ai platform, and became a SQL engine instead: Apache DataFusion for queries, plus local acceleration of datasets in Arrow or DuckDB. The company introduced it publicly in March 2024 as a SQL query engine to materialize and accelerate data from any database, warehouse or lake.

Over 2024 the project added search, model serving and an OpenAI-compatible API, and declared version 1.0 stable in January 2025, citing production use at Twilio and Barracuda Networks. Spice 2.0, in June 2026, moved beyond a single node with distributed queries on Apache Ballista, made the Vortex-based Cayenne accelerator generally available, and added direct CDC replication from operational databases.

choices.choice: Build on DataFusion instead of writing a query engine
choices.why: The Rust rewrite embedded Apache DataFusion from its first release (v0.7) for fast, standards-based SQL across sources. The company could then spend its effort on connectors, acceleration and AI features rather than on a planner and executor.

choices.choice: Materialize the working set next to the application
choices.why: Engines such as Trino and Dremio run as central clusters that many applications share. Spice usually runs one instance per application or tenant and keeps the data that app uses locally, trading extra copies for lower latency and less load on the source systems.

choices.choice: Let each dataset pick its accelerator
choices.why: No single storage engine suits every workload, so a dataset can use Arrow, DuckDB or Cayenne for analytical scans, or SQLite for transactional-style lookups, all behind the same SQL interface.

choices.choice: Drop model training from the open-source runtime
choices.why: The 2021 runtime bundled its own training engine. Version 0.7 removed it and the dashboard, leaving those to the hosted platform, so the open-source engine could focus on serving data to applications and models.

timeline.text: Spice AI founded; first alpha of a Go and Python runtime for time-series AI in August
Version 0.7 rewrites the runtime in Rust on DataFusion, in February
Version 2.0 in June: distributed queries on Ballista, Cayenne generally available, direct CDC
